subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house, because I think it will be of interest to the house, that Madame Vanier is leaving Ottawa tomorrow to establish permanent residence in Montreal. I know I am speaking for all members when I say that during her years at Rideau Hall she won a place in the hearts of Canadians that was equalled only by that which had been gained by her distinguished husband our beloved Governor General. The words I have used to try to express our admiration, affection and respect for the late Governor General apply equally, I am sure, to Madame Vanier. She was one half of a perfect partnership in service to Canada.
The house may also be interested to know that this evening at 6 p.m. Madame Vanier is to be sworn in as a member of the Privy Council of Canada. She will be the first woman, apart from ministers of the crown, to occupy that honourable place.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the announcement by the Prime Minister concerning the elevation of Madame Vanier to the Privy Council is something for which there will be general support. It is unusual, but it is entirely justified. Her grace, her charm, and above all the fact that she never lost sight of the people as a whole, or in other words her lack of stuffiness, gave to Rideau Hall a distinction by which the term of office of her late husband will always be remembered.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is significant that when members in all parts of this house and editorial writers across Canada were commenting on the passing of the late Governor General, almost without exception reference was made to the splendid contribution Madame Vanier had made during the years she and her husband had occupied Rideau Hall. I think therefore it is most fitting that this house should 23033-933J
pause in its deliberations to pay tribute to a very charming lady who brought to her position not only friendliness and kindliness, but also an intellectual capacity that enabled her to play an important role in the public life of Canada.
The Prime Minister is to be congratulated for having paid tribute to Madame Vanier by appointing her to the Privy Council. I am sure this gesture will be approved by Canadians in every walk of life. We think this honour well deserved and well earned. We wish Madame Vanier a long life, and we hope the gratitude of the Canadian people will always be for her an endearing memory.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we wish to congratulate the Prime Minister for appointing Madame Georges Vanier to the Privy Council. This is welcome news. In addition to bringing to its meetings her usual charm which parliament and all Canadians have come to know, I am sure that Madame Vanier will make a worthy contribution to the Privy Council. I feel that the Canadian people as a whole will be happy to hear about that appointment which will give even more weight to the Privy Council of Canada.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT TO CANADIAN PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we wish to associate ourselves with the words of appreciation to Madame Vanier for the splendid contribution she has made to Canada, and to join in the expression of best wishes as she leaves to establish residence in Montreal.

subtopic: TRIBUTE ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF JAMAICA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTE ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF JAMAICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regret I have to call the attention of the house to the passing an hour or so ago in Montreal of the recently elected prime minister of Jamaica. Sir Donald Sangster had been ill for some weeks in Montreal, and in spite of all the efforts of a great Canadian medical institution they were unable to save the life of this fine and noble man. He had served his country over the years with great distinction and devotion. He was the servant not only of Jamaica but of the commonwealth. My own feeling of regret is increased by the knowledge that I have lost one who was a good, personal friend.
I am sure the house will join me in expressing sympathy to the relatives of Sir Donald Sangster and to the people of Jamaica in the loss of their distinguished prime minister.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof-Mr. Hellyer- Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole to consider Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof. When the committee rose last evening clause 2 was under consideration.
On clause 2-Canadian forces, Canadian armed forces.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last night I was making a plea that the government modify its position with regard to the pressure it is placing on the house for a fast passage of Bill C-243. I pointed out that there existed across this country serious uncertainty as to what was involved in this legislation. I also pointed out that those all across this country who oppose this legislation or parts of it and who wish it to be modified depend on the opposition to press home their arguments and make the points which they wish to be made before this committee.
Speaking of uncertainty, we have to go back to the issuance of the white paper on defence which outlined the government's intention with regard to the reorganization of our Canadian armed forces. I think it is right
April 11, 1967	COMMONS
to assume that the government obtained the best advice they could at that time. They called in the military experts of this nation, questioned them and discussed the matter with them. On the basis of the information obtained they drew up the white paper. However, it has not been made clear even yet just what is intended to be the ultimate effect of the proposals published in that white paper.
Let us consider the two words, integration and unification. I am depending heavily for my argument on the testimony given before the standing committee of the house by Air Chief Marshal Miller. I know that Air Chief Marshal Miller's testimony has been freely quoted and I can well understand that. Of all the professional military witnesses called before the standing committee, the experience of Air Chief Marshal Miller probably qualified him as the best witness called.
For those who are not familiar with his career, if there are any here, Air Chief Marshal Miller served from 1931 to 1955 in the R.C.A.F. He was a professional soldier. I think it is agreed by everyone that he was a professional soldier of the highest type, one of whom all Canadians can be proud. He was one of many such who were called before the standing committee. From 1955 to 1960 Air Chief Marshal Miller served as deputy minister of the Department of National Defence. If there is any place where any man can acquire more valuable experience than in the post of deputy minister of the department, I cannot imagine it. From 1960 to 1964 Air Chief Marshal Miller served as chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, as long as that body existed. When the joint chiefs of staff were abolished and responsibility was turned over to a single chief of staff as part of the integration program, Air Chief Marshal Miller was given that responsible position. He served as chief of staff from 1964 until 1966 when he retired.
There was no evidence produced to indicate that relations between Air Chief Marshal Miller and the government or the minister were anything but most cordial and most cooperative. Air Chief Marshal Miller defined integration as a force having a single defence staff, a single planning staff and a single budget procedure.
The program of integration, in contrast to unification, is widely supported. I think we can say it has been unanimously accepted by all of the officers and specialists in the defence department. Air Chief Marshal Miller defined unification as a single force having a
National Defence Act Amendment single rank structure, a single administrative chain of command, a common uniform and a force wherein the trades and ranks would be called by common names. Air Chief Marshal Miller stated, as recorded on page 2326 of the committee evidence, that when the program began unification and integration were interchangeably used. These words were accepted as having approximately the same meaning. It was only when the program got well along that a differentiation was made between the meaning of these two words.
As Air Chief Marshal Miller pointed out in his definition, integration called for a single defence staff, one commander and one chief of staff rather than the three members of the joint chiefs of staff including the chairman. Instead of having three chains of command as we formerly had, there was to be one chain of command, one single administrative chain. There was to be a single planning staff, that is, you would have a commander of planning and one staff serving the three branches of the armed forces. In addition, there would be a single budget procedure. The budget for all our Canadian armed forces would be handled through one organization, one budget planning board. Now, this is acceptable to practically everyone.
Later a proposal was made that unification should take place. Unification has boiled down to the abolition of the three branches of the service, the army, navy and air force, through reorganization into one force under one commander, having a common uniform and with the trades and ranks called by common names. It was at this point that very serious opposition arose across this country. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that instead of diminishing this opposition is increasing. I plead with the government and I plead with the minister to take note of this fact. There is no reason, at least no evidence has been submitted by the experts in the field, why the government cannot stop now, having accomplished a very substantial measure of integration quite apart from what is now called unification.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Let the government stop now and subject the present state of integration to a substantial trial period. It can be tried out for whatever time iis required, six months or a year. Some of the experts suggested from three to five years, and some even longer than that. The present state of integration should be thoroughly proved, I suggest, before we go on with what is now known as unification.

As for the advantages and disadvantages of stopping now or proceeding further, again I should like to quote from Air Chief Marshal Miller's evidence because as I have already indicated X do not think there could be any more valuable evidence. From the standpoint of experience and qualifications the Air Chief Marshal was more adequately fitted to provide information than anybody else. The testimony he gave did not stand out by itself. The testimony he gave-he was one of the last witnesses to be called by the committee-substantiated evidence which had been repeated by witness after witness among that talented array of military specialists whom the committee invited to appear before them.
We do not need to stop on this side of the water for evidence in this regard, because in the Montreal Gazette for Saturday last, April 8, Admiral Mountbatten was drawn into the controversy. He did not want to be drawn into the controversy and there was no inclination on his part to interfere in Canadian political affairs, but he sent a clarifying statement from London after he had been advised by Richard H. Gaunt, a retired Canadian naval officer, that he was being represented in Canada as an all-out supporter of unification. Admiral Mountbatten made his position clear, and if we want the evidence of a disinterested specialist, surely his evidence would qualify as such.
As reported in this issue of the Montreal Gazette, Admiral Mountbatten stated:
"Few people still oppose the integration of arrangements for pay, food, clothing, furniture, equipment, etc., since this must be a more economical way of providing them," he said in his statement...
Admiral Mountbatten pointed out, however, that in the British reorganization, great care had been taken to preserve morale and service tradition.
One of the chief complaints of the opposition at this time is that the government has not paid sufficient attention to the wishes of the personnel in the armed forces. Then the article continues with this direct quotation from Admiral Mountbatten:
"It has been accepted that to achieve this"-
I assume he means integration.
-"the three services must retain their uniforms and ranks with an identifiable professional head of their service," he said. "The idea of a single uniform and rank structure was also rejected as undesirable and unnecessary".
The Montreal Gazette felt so strongly about the matter that this morning's issue carried an editorial on the question. Part of it reads as follows:
Lord Mountbatten, too, is an advocate of unified command and integration of services ...

But integration and unification are two quite different things. Both men-
There the article is referring to Admiral Mountbatten and Air Chief Marshal Miller.
-come down strongly against haste in creating a single service with a single uniform.
Lord Mountbatten confirmed there was some talk of unifying the services in Britain, but it was turned down as "undesirable, unnecessary and"-
I am sure the minister will not like the last word.
-"ludicrous."
"No compensating advantages could be seen in attempting to impose so unpopular a change," he said.
Air Marshal Miller, speaking on the advantages and disadvantages of unification, said:
"I said I did not see a monetary return for unification, nor do I see any significant military effectiveness. I said I saw some unanswered questions associated with unification that perhaps should be spelled out before you could really get out and sell it to people."
These are honest doubts, honestly expressed. And they are grounds for caution in adopting in Canada a policy that can bring no monetary return, and which might be unnecessary, if not ludicrous.
There is evidence, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that there may be disadvantages. As reported at page 2297 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence, Air Chief Marshal Miller was asked this question:
Do you, yourself, see any financial advantage accruing from the proposed scheme of unification?
Again, there they are talking about unification as opposed to integration. Air Chief Marshal Miller replied:
There are no significant financial advantages whatsoever as far as I can see.
He was then asked this question:
Do you see any military advantages flowing from it?
He replied:
Again, there are no significant military advantages.
So there are no financial advantages and there are no significant military advantages. If the best expert in the field makes statements of this kind, Mr. Chairman, surely the government should pay some attention to them.
Again he was asked:
Do you see any military disadvantages coming out of it?
Air Chief Marshal Miller replied:
The disruption is an unknown factor, and one which I have always rated rather highly.
April 11, 1967	COMMONS
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I do not know whether the word "highly" is a good word here. It might be interpreted as meaning that perhaps there is something commendable about this possible disruption, though quite evidently Air Chief Marshal Miller did not mean anything of the sort. He indicated that the disruption which might result from unification is an unknown factor and one which he had always rated rather highly or of great importance. He went on to say:
I did not want to have anything occur that would cause disruption in the services. I felt a lot of careful planning was necessary, and that probably time to educate people was required before the next step of unification was taken.
There we have the advice of the leading expert in the field, a man who has served long and faithfully in our armed forces, a man better qualified than anybody else to speak.
I felt a lot of careful planning was necessary, and that probably time to educate people was required before the next step of unification was taken.
That theme was repeated a number of times by other witnesses. I will not repeat their evidence because there is not enough time. Parts of their evidence have been quoted freely and widely.
I suggest to the government and the minister that a case has not been made out to show why we should not stop this process of unification, if one can call it that, at the present stage of integration. It has not been shown that it would be unwise to stop the process. Air Chief Marshal Miller and many other witnesses said that we should thoroughly test the process of integration for a period of years before taking the drastic step of wiping out our three services and combining them, with one uniform and a common rank structure. There is evidence to show that the prospect of unification is upsetting the morale of the troops and is disturbing people from one end of the country to the other. I suggest to the government that if there is no sound reason for not stopping the integration process now and testing it thoroughly before going on, the government should stop it and allow us to get on with the other business of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I begin what I hope will be my brief remarks with a sincere thank you to my friends on both sides of the house who sent their good wishes while I was in hospital recently and who welcomed me back to the house so kindly. To be personal
National Defence Act Amendment for a moment, my condition turned out to be a temporary one at this time. I found from speaking to other members that a great many of us in this chamber have had a similar experience. I do thank you all and I hope that other members, if or when their turn comes -and I hope and pray it will not-will have as happy an outcome as mine was.
While I was away some remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops appeared in one form or another in the press. I again wish to express my thanks to my hon. friends on both sides of the house who in this instance took up the cudgels on my behalf. I do appreciate it but I would like to go on to say that, having read a few days ago in the Victoria Times a further interview with the hon. member for Kamloops, I wish to clear the air right away and say that I accept without any reservation whatsoever his explanation of what it was he had in mind in the first instance. Part of the basis for the hon. member's remarks was that I was worried about unification. "Concerned" might better have described my feelings for, of course, I am concerned about unification. Aren't we all? That is what we are here for today; this is our job at this moment.
Unification is a big thing for Canada. When parliament entrusted the defence committee with the study of the bill on unification and its implications, surely it then became our task to hear evidence, to work on the bill and if possible to make it a better bill. That is what committees are for and that is what we did. We all became concerned about the bill.
While I am on my feet and in a thanking mood, Mr. Chairman, I hope you will allow me to use this opportunity to thank the very patient members of the defence committee who laboured with me as their chairman for most of the past 12 months. In particular I want to thank the steering committee which included, of course, the hon. member for Edmonton West, the vice chairman of the committee, and the hon. member for Vancouver East who always had a fair contribution to make to our committee's deliberations.
Let me say a word or two before I go on about the witnesses who appeared before our committee. I, of course, heard all those who appeared before my sudden departure and I think I have read all that was said by those who appeared subsequently. I know you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that we are indeed a favoured land when our nation can command the services of such men. I am not pretending that I agreed with all that was said but,
April 11, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment without exception, the witnesses had something valuable to contribute and they put forward their case with a sincerity that no one could doubt and with a dignity we can all envy.
I will not speak at length about the deliberations of the committee, the number of witnesses, the pages of evidence or even about the number of words as ascertained by some keen mathematical mind, which have been spoken on the subject. I will, however, describe to the house what I think are some far-reaching implications of this debate. Since last July and particularly in recent weeks thousands of words and endless repetition have been the order of the day on the precise definition of unification and what it means, and I think this has constituted a good part of the problem which we members and the public have faced. There is, of course, no such word as unification in the dictionary in a military sense, and I am sure in my own mind the Minister of National Defence will never again coin a new word to describe such a far-reaching and, if I may add my own view, such a far-seeing operation as that which is now before us in this bill. Since the word has no definitive military meaning we have been left to our own devices to interpret it in our own way.
My personal definition or view, which incidentally is the same today as when I started considering the matter many months ago, is that when we speak of unification we are talking about taking integration as far as it is practical to go. I understand my own definition, which is hardly surprising, but what is far more important, the people I talk to can also understand it and see more clearly what it is we are trying to do. From here on in my speech, then, I shall refer to what is before us as the integration-unification bill or process.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I think it is of the greatest importance when speaking on this matter to emphasize the following point, that the planning for integration-unification will be done by the men in the armed forces themselves. The minister has said so, and that, of course, is how it should be. It is the servicemen who will be affected by it so it is only right that they themselves should be the ones to draw the route to be travelled toward the general objective which will be given to them by parliament, I hope very shortly. Furthermore, regardless of what has been said here by both proponents and opponents of the plan, the very fact that the planning will be done by

those who will both execute the plan and live with it is a guarantee, at least to me, that they will have a very large measure of control over the speed of execution of the plan. In addition, it is a guarantee to me that the plan in its final form will be a good one, coming as it will from men of such experience, ability and good sense as those who appeared as service witnesses before the committee.
The minister has not denied that in its final form the integration-unification plan may look a lot different from what it does now. He has told us he takes no immutable stand on the details, and there are few hard and fast details in the bill itself. One of the opponents of the bill, referring to the lack of planning, likened it to a man proceeding down a road in a dense fog, going from lamp post to lamp post. I have no argument with that. I find it a good simile. It all depends, of course, on whether you know where you are going and whether or not you start out on the right road. I believe we are on the right road and that we do know our objective, and I can imagine no better way of proceeding along this ill-defined thoroughfare than by taking easy steps from one recognizable point to the next. Is this not precisely what the service planners have been telling us they are doing, and in the bill before us is the government not asking for permission to continue this orderly planning progression toward the integration-unification objective?
In a task of this magnitude, particularly when it involves entering areas hitherto unexplored, areas where hidden dangers may well lurk, there will unquestionably be changes of route and method. But what of that? Does this mean that the task is one which should not be attempted at all simply because we do not know all the answers in advance? Must we Canadians really be, as Marshall McLuhan has described us-he is not an air marshal and, indeed, has nothing to do with anyone's armed forces - must we Canadians really be "mildewed with caution" as he said we are? I do not think so. We have been accused of destroying things which should be preserved. That is not our objective. We are not setting out to destroy anything.

We are, however, trying to build something new and in the process of
April 11, 1967	COMMONS
building some things, some good things, I admit, have to be changed. Take the uniform. Much has been said about it but, no matter what has been said, service uniforms are not being completely removed. To emphasize the permanency of the integration-unification arrangements and the interpendence of those who serve in the new organizations it is proposed, however, that on many occasions all officers and men should wear what is basically the same uniform. What is wrong with that? It makes sense to me. I could certainly live with that arrangement. It means a change, but that is how things go. We see this sort of thing happening in all fields of life, so an explanation or apology is scarcely needed from me. It is a fact of life, and we have to keep up with the pace of life if we are to survive.
I believe this bill before us, this imaginative bill is one good example that Canadians are not always, to quote McLuhan again, "looking into the rear-view mirror and defending the status quo, which is outmoded the moment it happens." If in the process of opposing the bill we carry our objections beyond the realm of fact into the lush, tempting fields of speculation and fancy, it could well be a disaster for us all. For example, were the armed forces of Canada to become demoralized by protracted debate and ridicule lightly heaped upon this new idea by this house, we would all suffer.
Those responsible for a debate of that sort would have to be ready to shoulder a heavy responsibility. Can they be as sure of themselves in their objections as they claim in this house to be? I doubt it very, very much. Hon. members and others need no reminder from me that in the armed forces of Canada we are dealing with a group of volunteers who traditionally and rightly shun the limelight, who do the peoples' bidding without question and who voluntarily forgo, because of their love of Queen, country and adventure, a great many of the democratic safeguards which we civilians prize and about which we so endlessly boast. There would be no such freedom if there were no such armed forces in the free world. In return these men ask very little, but what they demand is sensible direction and at least some understanding by public and parliament alike of what their problems are. I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that this house is in the process of creating, if it has not already partly created, a problem of morale in the armed forces which requires active consideration by all of us as members of parliament.

I would prefer to deal with questions at the conclusion of my brief remarks. A goodly portion of the comment in the House of Commons, in the press and outside the house has somewhat naturally been concentrated on the negative aspects of integration-unification. It could hardly be otherwise. But there comes a time when such comments have side effects far greater than were ever perhaps intended. If you keep telling a person he is sick, sooner or later he starts believing it. If this were to happen in our armed services, we would all be in trouble and every member in this house would share the blame.
Various hon. members on the opposite side have painted a dismal picture of the morale situation today within the Canadian armed forces and in particular in the Royal Canadian Navy on the east coast. I can only say that this does not fit in with the impressions I get from across the country and the position as I see it from the point of view of the R.C.N. on the west coast. Of course, there always were two navies in the Royal Canadian Navy-the east coast navy and the west coast navy. And I am quite sure that if things on the east coast are as bad as they are being painted by the hon. member for Halifax, then subject to the Minister of National Defence making a few new arrangements with NATO, which should not be too hard to do, the west coast navy will cheerfully take over some of the Halifax or east coast obligations and show once again in a spirit of friendly competition, the spirit which so often exists in this house, that anything they can do in Halifax we can do better in Esquimalt. In fact I think there really is a need within the R.C.N. for a readjustment in the division of the strength of the navy between the east and the west coast of Canada. Surely present events across the ocean in China and in other countries bordering the Pacific rim are convincing evidence enough to warrant such a change, and I ask the minister to give it his serious consideration.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In recent years the east coast navy has not, to my knowledge, been up to full strength. For years and years it has had to borrow sometimes reluctant sailors from the west coast navy. This is no reflection on any admiral, least of all on Admiral O'Brien, now maritime commander in Halifax, who must know that for many years he has had my
April 11. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment admiration and respect. He has, among other things, a tough problem with bad weather and lots of snow, which makes the west coast look pretty attractive to some sailors.
So much has been said about changes in uniform and so forth that I feel I must make some further comment and, if hon. members will permit me, I would like to say that within my own experience naval officers in particular over the years have been overly conservative in matters of changes of dress. For example, ask any old sailor what happened when in 1941, I think it was, we were issued with the Canadian Volunteer Service Medal with its little silver maple leaf to denote Canadian volunteers on overseas service. Many of us just did not wear it because it was different and other navies did not have one. This is true.
Ask old sailors about the time we were directed to wear "Canada" flashes on the shoulders of our uniforms to denote what country we were from. Once again there was great hostility to this, and for many months many officers just did not make the change.
What about the red maple leaf painted on the funnels of R.C.N. ships, an idea that spread like wildfire throughout Canadian ships abroad once someone thought of it? We were ordered to take it off, and on my ship -incidentally this was overseas so I do not know who was responsible for ordering it to be taken off-we went through a period of finding that it had been painted anonymously on the funnel by night and being obliged officially to paint it out by day. What a farcical situation that was. I remind hon. members that it was not until the war was over that this distinctive emblem was permitted to become official, and of course it has remained official until the present day and will not be changed under this bill.
Again, you should have heard the uproar in some quarters when, as a result of representation by the sailors, the navy's traditional tot of rum was allowed to be issued mixed with a cola drink instead of water. What a catastrophe that was going to be. Nelson wouldn't have liked it. As a matter of fact I think he would have liked it because he was a very progressive admiral.
I will not try to describe the feeling in some quarters when it was discovered that zippers were to be incorporated into the naval uniform, and would you believe that diagonal serge cloth for sailors' uniforms would cause any heartburn in anyone? Well, it did and many is the old sailor who will recall he was

ordered to dispose of his "tiddley" uniform because he had had it made ashore of light weight comfortable diagonal woven serge. It wasn't quite regulation then but it is regulation now.
If hon. members are not too tired of these matters I can go on. We even put a zipper on the sailor's jumper. But here it turned out we were making progress. When we dared to put zippers on the sailors' jumpers the Royal Navy copied us, but it was not until they did so that suspicion of this innovation completely disappeared in some quarters of the R.C.N.

For a moment I would like to talk about the rift which has undoubtedly and quite understandably been caused by the integration-unification process and all that it entails or, rightly or wrongly, appears to entail in the minds of its supporters and detractors. This, as we have seen, covers a whole heap of territory, as you, Mr. Chairman, might say in more grammatical terms. The rift extends beyond the service and well into civilian life. It is there and it bodes ill for the future of the armed forces if something is not done about it and done fairly quickly. I place the blame for a great deal of this on a quite unbelievable lack of understanding as to what it is we are trying to do. Even today I hear people, who should and in fact do know better, talking as if we were trying to turn over servicemen into all-purpose fighting paragons. Soldiers in kilts, climbing the rigging of ships-what utter nonsense! It is sad, but it is perhaps indicative of the lengths to which otherwise normal, rational people go when they are confronted with highly charged emotional matters in which they are very much personally involved. I do not blame them unduly.
Speaking personally, before we had the facts and were dealing with wild rumours I found some difficulty myself in being impartial and unbiased. But this is not the case today. Apart from pointing out that the vast majority of these rumours subsequently turned out to be quite false, I should also say that there was much about the old organization and the old way of doing things which we are now trying to change with which I
April 11, 1967

also disagreed and disagreed even more strongly. On balance I think I can say that from the start I have been in favour of the idea behind integration and unification, and now that integration-unification is with us I want to see it work in the best possible way.
How can we overcome the rift about which I speak and how can we best go about it after this bill in its final form is passed, as I believe it shortly will be? It may be of interest to some hon. members to know that in other countries' armed services in modern times there have been other emotional cataclysms and even deeper-seated rifts than in our own, but the unbeatable combination of good will and intelligence has healed the wounds. I cannot believe that we lack in Canada, particularly among those who are affected and are interested in integration-unification, either intelligence or good will. So I think we are going to come out of this situation in good shape all right.
Since the service which seems to have been zeroed in on, if I may use that expression, is the navy, I would draw the attention of hon. members to a situation which developed in the Royal Navy of Great Britain not long before world war I when Great Britain's far-flung empire covered so much of the globe and the Royal Navy was quite realistically called "Britain's sure shield" and was very largely responsible not only for defending the empire against all comers and all combinations of comers but also for policing the farthest corners of the empire's interests.
The schism in this case developed over a difference of opinion between two senior admirals, Fisher and Beresford, both very popular and both men of ideas and integrity. Fisher was the more senior of the two and he became the first sea lord of the British Admiralty. He was a reformer, and I think it is fair to say that in the light of history it can be seen that the great majority of his reforms have stood the test of time and, had they not been put into effect, the British Royal Navy would not have been as well prepared as it was when in 1914 and again in 1939 it was called into action. Many of the innovations Lord Fisher introduced, and he produced quite a few, are still with us today. Fisher had his supporters. Beresford, on the other hand, had his.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I will not go into the details, although there are many books in the parliamentary library which cover this subject. Those who are fond of history and who seek literary diversion

National Defence Act Amendment could do worse than spend an hour or two following the course of this dispute. I am sure they will be struck by the quite astounding similarity between the development of recent events in Canada and those engendered by the Fisher-Beresford dispute. Many of the points put forward by both sides were equally contrived. Many of their fears turned out to be just as groundless and many of their methods were quite as farcical as some we have witnessed. I will stop there in the interest of time.
I am interested in bringing to the attention of the committee the aftermath of the controversy in Britain, the rift and the damage to naval and military discipline because, believe it or not, the dispute was still being talked about in the British navy when I arrived on the scene some 25 or 30 years later. In my opinion we can make no better start to mend this rift of ours than by getting on with our job of dealing with the clause by clause study of the bill and voting on it. Let us remove the heavy, deadly pall of uncertainty which now hangs over the armed forces. Let the servicemen know for certain where they are going. At least let parliament set the objective and let the armed forces get on with their job of planning their own route and timetable in order to get there.
To the members of this house I have this to say: In a venture as imaginative and far reaching as this I am glad to have a part. I happen to be playing my part today in the House of Commons, but with this sort of challenge I feel so strongly about this bill and what it will do for Canada that I would return willingly tomorrow to the navy, if they would have me, at my old or any lesser rank -I am not fussy. You can see from the amount of weight I am losing that I am getting ready to fit into some of my old uniforms. I am not just saying this, I mean it, and I know there are others who feel the same way. I mention this only to point out that there are many ex-servicemen who are as anxious as I to see this all-Canadian venture succeed and who are anxious to give Canada another "first" in the military field and another mark of prestige in international circles.
All hon. members now have a hand in this important measure. In speaking to hon. members opposite I should like to say that this is a better and more practical bill today than it was when it went to the committee, not that there were any changes made in the committee while I was there but rather changes made later by the members and by my
April 11, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment successor as chairman. There may possibly be other improvements still to be made. How can we tell unless we get into the clause by clause discussion?
The opposition undoubtedly has a duty to perform and as everyone knows I have never questioned that. But I am questioning it now. There is considerable, though as I have said perhaps unintentional, danger if we persist with this debate much longer. I think it can rightly be claimed that the opposition has played the game and has put up a fair fight with tangible and valuable results, but the time has come when we must get on with our task as parliamentarians and our job of making a decision. It may be difficult but we cannot delay it forever. The government has the responsibility and is prepared both to assume its responsibility and stand by the consequences. There are other consequences to be borne in throwing up a roadblock and stalemating this debate and for these the opposition has to judge its own responsibility.

I do not know who made the decision-I do not know whether it was made by the right hon. gentleman himself or by the late Senator Brunt, but someone made the decision and it was promulgated.

The strike role was the military choice. It was accepted by the government of the right hon. gentleman. What I find disturbing about the current discussions regarding unification of the armed forces is that there seems to be little, if any, reference to the basic principles involved.
The bitter arguments revolve around uniforms, ancient history and personal emotions.
Broadly speaking, the advantages of unification can be summed up as unity of purpose and, secondly, cohesiveness.
Unity of purpose from top to bottom, has growing significance with the development of modern and changing weapons and conditions. It

has special relevance to the modern problem of "limited war"- the form of war (other than "peace-keeping") which is likely to involve Canada.
Cohesiveness ensures maximum effort in the direction of the desired "purpose". It includes such factors as the power to implement decisions in a comprehensive manner; ability to concentrate effort; flexibility; improved communications; effective economy in use of manpower and equipment, etc.
The commonest objections to unification are the anticipated difficulties in connection with expansion of part or all of the armed forces (if needed); ability, or lack of it, to co-operate with allies; morale.
For all major expansion the problems of unified and separate forces would be largely the same. This, therefore, is not a valid objection, as the scales tip somewhat in favour of unification.
Co-operation with allies, always difficult, seems to present no greater difficulties one way or the other.
Morale is the most important single thing in war. Many things go to make up morale but the one overwhelmingly important single factor is leadership.

All these things call for modernization of the armed forces set-up. Canada with its small armed forces is in an ideal position to do this.

I am encouraged to say a few more words on this bill because of the intervention by certain people of some importance on the other side of the house. The chairman of the defence committee, the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.), spoke earlier, and the Minister of Transport intervened on Friday. Once the Minister of Transport enters a debate like this one, it is wide open for anyone to speak because I do not know of any person on the government side who knows less about this particular matter than does the Minister of Transport. Then there was the intervention on Wednesday of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, a contribution which deserves some attention. Today we heard from the Minister of National Defence.
I think it is important that in a debate there should be an exchange of opinions. This is what debate is. Arguments are put forward by one side or the other. Whether or not opinions are changed in the course of these discussions is an open question. But I do know that a great many members of the House of Commons, to say nothing of the public, have learned much more about the unification bill than they knew before.
We have heard people announcing that a great many meetings of the defence committee were held and that a number of witnesses were heard, and that in these circumstances all that remains is for the issue to be decided here by a vote. I submit to you, sir, that all

members of parliament should have an opportunity to find out what happened in the committee. Not every member of parliament has the time to read the voluminous reports which are prepared by committees, and sometimes a member will benefit by hearing a summary of what has transpired in a committee. I do that here, and have for many years. I do not serve on all the committees but I like to hear from members who serve on committees. I listen to their reports to the house, just what they amount to, and then if I am in doubt about some matter I refer to the detailed committee proceedings. This goes on all the time.
I found a great deal of interest not so long ago in hearing the debate on the transportation bill, one of the most important bills to come before the House of Commons in recent years. The committee on transportation had an enormous number of meetings. It heard expert evidence. We have been encouraged in the present debate to pay no attention to expert evidence. The committee on transportation had a different view. It called in experts and listened to them very carefully. Then the bill came before the house, having been amended to quite an extent in the committee, and was later amended in the house.

That debate was very interesting. A great deal of information was put in front of us, to such an extent that I found it was possible for me to participate in the debate, which I did, and the Minister of Transport will recall that it was on my initiative he got tripped up over the clause on the Crowsnest Pass rates and suffered what he later termed a humiliation-and it was, because he was very careless.
I give that as an example of what should be done following the meetings of committees. A committee brings back a report to the house. The members sitting in at committee hearings have an obligation to give a report to the House of Commons in order that other members who have not participated in the committee hearings may get a summary of what was done there. Then you have the other aspect of it, that there are members of the House of Commons who, for one reason or another, do not serve on committees in which they are interested but who have a great deal of knowledge of the subject matter before those committees, and those members should have the opportunity to debate the issues in the House of Commons. That is precisely the course of this debate. We have spent several

days on it, but not any more than are required, because of the nature of the subject and its importance.
An opportunity has been presented for members of the defence committee to state the case in the House of Commons, and there is an opportunity for other members who were not on that committee to express their views on this vital matter. Over and above that, each member of the House of Commons hopes that somebody somewhere in the general public will hear something about his views and perhaps be influenced by them.
I also think that in this particular matter of defence we have an obligation to speak on behalf of those people who cannot be heard, who have not the privilege of making their voices heard. That applies to all the people within the services, because under their regulations they do not have the privilege of making public speeches.
There is a widespread discontent within the services, and those of us who are aware of that think we are duty bound to bring it to the attention of the government and to the attention of the people of Canada. If not, you hear only one side. You hear only from the minister, telling the public that everything is fine within the services. Those of us on this side of the chamber know perfectly well that that is not the case. We have had too much information given to us, in one way or another, to show that there is massive discontent within the services and that it has been occasioned by the action of the government.
In the defence committee we drew attention to the very large number of officers who left the services prior to their normal retirement. Many of those people left the services because they were told by the minister that they either had to go along with his proposal or get out. A great number of junior officers left the services early because of what they saw going on-uncertainty in the Department of National Defence, too many respected senior officers fired out of hand, and great doubt as to the future in the services.
During the course of the committee hearings I had occasion to discuss with one of the witnesses the number of personnel who had passed through national defence headquarters. I think that in the space of two years 3,000 officers had passed through national defence headquarters: I call it Grand Central Station. A great number of those officers left the services entirely; others were shifted back and forth. I do not know of any business that could operate efficiently with such a large
National Defence Act Amendment personnel turnover; and yet under the minister that is what was going on at national defence headquarters.
It is no wonder that General Fleury said he could not stand it any longer. He did not know from one day to the next what officers were going to be working with him at headquarters. That is the type of chaos created by the minister. It is quite proper that this should be brought to the attention of members of the house and to the attention of the public.
The trouble stems from the erratic behavior of the minister and his impetuosity to get this particular bill passed at the present time. I think he selected this as his centennial project. He had to think of something, and last summer he decided this would be his centennial project and he would end up in 1967 with a newly designed defence force, a unified force. Otherwise I cannot see any reason for the haste, because all the advice that was given to him was to the contrary.
The senior officers, even those still serving, have said, "Give us more time to work out the aspects of integration. We need more time to straighten out materiel command," which takes in the supply end of it. They have said "We need more time on Training Command." and there is the greatest doubt in the world as to whether Training Command is going to work, and work effectively.
The minister brushes all this aside as inconsequential. The people actually working at the job do not find it inconsequential at all; they find it a very difficult task. They are worried about the consequences, and if an emergency comes upon us this year, I have the gravest doubts as to whether the present organization could effectively meet that emergency. I think the minister would be forced back to the older system of three services.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, the chairman of the defence committee in its later stages, who operated moderately effectively after we had given him instruction as to how to conduct committee hearings, reported to the house yesterday with regard to this bill and made what I consider to be the most astonishing statement I have heard with regard to it. At page 14714 of yesterday's Hansard you find these immortal words of his:
Only one thing of any real importance remained to be done and that was to give the new single force which we had created in 1964 a name. Bill C-243 asks us to do that. No clause in Bill C-243. other than clause 2 before the committee now, is of any real significance. I say that because clause 2 gives the force a new name.

National Defence Act Amendment
Not content with a ridiculous statement like that, he repeated it about seven minutes later. That comes from the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, who acted as chairman of that committee. It comes from the man who reported to the house that there had been 55 meetings and 38 witnesses heard. He said that the only purpose of the bill was to give the forces a new name. Well, if his words are accurate, there has been a terrible waste of time here in parliament and in committee. But of course his words are absolutely inaccurate.

Far from just giving the forces a new name, the bill destroys the three services, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force, and substitutes another force for those three. Clause 2 of the bill to which he referred does that by amending the present act, striking out those names, and making one service called the Canadian Armed Forces.
A little further on this same clause provides for the creation of a special force. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra did not mention that but I intend to mention it. Further on in the bill-and we will be coming to this later on-clause 6 provides for the compulsory transfer of the people now in the navy, army and air force into the single service, the Canadian Armed Forces.
Now, Mr. Chairman, one can readily realize the absolutely erroneous impression given by the chairman of that committee to the house when he spoke yesterday and said that it was just a simple little matter of changing the name. That is not so at all. On this side of the house we have said that we should retain the three services, work away at the integrated side of it, and see whether we can make a success of it. In 1964 I had doubts concerning that and opposed the legislation right down to third reading, just as I am opposing this. I still have in my mind a big question mark with regard to integration itself.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: You are consistent.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
If I can be shown that it can be successful in respect of the integration of the supply forces and so on, then I am prepared to accept integration. I believe, however, that it is wrong to have just one chief of staff. I do not intend to repeat the argument I used in 1964, but I believe, now when integration has not been effected, it is foolish to go ahead with unification.
The bill of course does more than just change a name. It wipes out the three services and makes one service. We have been told that everybody in that one service will be-although not called sailors, soldiers and airmen-working quite a bit either at sea, on the land or in the air. We have been told there will be no transfer of people from one area to another. This is not accurate, because this clause 2 with which we are dealing, modifies section 17 of the original act. I will read the words:
In an emergency, or if considered desirable in consequence of any action undertaken by Canada under the United Nations Charter, the North Atlantic Treaty or any other similar instrument for collective defence entered into by Canada, the governor in council may establish and authorize the maintenance of a component of the Canadian forces, referred to in this Act as the special force . . .
If this is passed the power will be given to the department and to the minister to create a special force. In that special force may be placed any person, officer or man, from the unified force. It does not state that those who have had their training at sea, in the air or on the land will not be required to serve elsewhere than in the area in which they received their training; it does not say that at all. It says that a special force may be created and in that force will be placed officers and men of the regular force. There is no protection here at all. There is nothing which states that a man who has been trained only for land operations will not have to serve at sea, or vice-versa. Yet, we have been told that none of this will happen.
As I say, right there in this bill is the evidence that it will be possible for the minister and his staff to do this. When the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said that all this bill did was to change the name he omitted to draw the attention of the house to clause 6 to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred so effectively.
Why did the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, the chairman of the committee, not frankly tell the members of this house that in clause 6 a compulsory feature had been introduced which borders on conscription. This is a feature which will affect very seriously the officers and men now serving in the three separate services, because once this bill has passed the house and the Senate and has been proclaimed, it will become the law. On its becoming law some of the officers and men who now are in the Royal Canadian Navy will cease to be in the Royal Canadian Navy and will become members of the defence force,
(Mr. Churchill.]
April 11, 1967	COMMONS
and the officers and men who now are in the Royal Canadian Air Force will cease to be in that branch of the service and will become members of the defence force. The same will be true of the army. They will not have a choice. We brought this up during the committee hearings. We argued with the minister about this. We asked him whether he was going to give the men now in the present services a choice as to whether or not they would go into this newly styled single force, and he said no. He says no to almost everything.
I pointed out the experience we had in September of 1939. I appreciate the fact that I am not supposed to refer to any of the wars which have taken place in the past, but I will take the chance again. On September 1, 1939, when we were enlisting men in the Fort Garry Horse we signed them on into the Canadian field force. They were enlisted and attested into that force-the Canadian field force. In two or three days word came from Ottawa that a new title had been selected. That new title was the Canadian Active Service Force. It was necessary to reattest those men into that force.
Then, somewhat later, word was sent to us that under the Canadian Active Service Force there was no compulsion to serve outside the boundaries of Canada. Therefore it was necessary to take a third step. The officers and men were asked whether they wished to serve abroad. It was necessary again for them to indicate their desire by signing their signature. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South has pointed out, that was done in wartime and quite conceivably the cabinet of that period could have said, "Well, we have organized the Canadian field force and since we want to change the name to the Canadian Active Service Force, we will do it by order in council and that will be that, and all those who have enlisted to date will be automatically in the Canadian Active Service Force". Even in wartime, the government used its common sense and said that the men, having been attested into the Canadian field force, with that name being changed, would have the opportunity of saying whether or not they wanted to be in the Canadian Active Service Force. The government of that day did not say everyone in the Canadian Active Service Force must serve anywhere in the world. That government gave the officers and men a chance to make their own decision.
National Defence Act Amendment [DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I hope it never happens, but if this bill becomes law and is proclaimed I hope the minister will give the officers and men of the three services an opportunity to say whether or not they want to serve in this new force and, if they do not want to serve in it, let them be retired or honourably discharged without any reduction in the pension to which they may be entitled at that time. These officers and men are all volunteers and this is how they should be treated. When we discussed this in the committee, the minister rejected the idea. That is another example of the typical, arrogant and domineering attitude of this Liberal government.
Let me indicate why this is important. The men presently serving in the three services made a decision when they enlisted in those three services. Some men went to the recruiting officers and said they wanted to serve in the army, while others said they wanted to serve at sea with the navy, or perhaps with the air force. Many of them have made a deliberate choice in this regard. Some people do not like the ocean and are not very comfortable at sea. I happen to be one of those. Some people do not want to fly and would much prefer to serve on land in a particular unit of the land forces. Very often the men in the army will make a specific choice. Perhaps they do not wish to be in the armoured corps because it means they will be shut up in a tank. Perhaps they suffer from claustrophobia. Thousands of people during the second world war had no use at all for the armoured corps from the standpoint of serving in it, because they did not want to be shut up in a tank, where they could burn to death if it was hit by a shell. Similarly some people in the navy do not want to serve in submarines.
All these people should be given a choice. But that is not the plan for this 1967 centennial arrangement. The officers and men will have no choice, but will be compulsorily placed in this new force. As I pointed out, if a special force is formed in an emergency, these men may be transferred at will from one branch to another.
In answer to the suggestion by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, that there was only one major change in this bill, I pointed out three. These changes involved the wiping out of the three services-the navy, army and air force; the creation, if necessary, of a special force to which anyone may be posted as the staff or minister sees fit, and the
April 11, 1987

National Defence Act Amendment automatic and compulsory conscription of these men from the navy, army and air force into one defence force. That gives you some idea as to why there is opposition to this bill.
The minister has given no indication of a willingness to yield on any aspect of this bill. In this respect he differs from the Minister of Forestry, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and the Minister of Transport. I do not have any less admiration in this regard for those men, but I do know from their work in this house that they have modified bills at the request of the opposition, or when it became apparent that they were running into too much difficulty.
Perhaps I have said enough in respect of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I should not have spent so much time dealing with his remarks, because really they are not deserving of any attention at all. I intend to pass over the references I was going to make regarding the Minister of Transport, and I shall do so with one exception. That minister interrupted the hon. member for Calgary North as reported at page 14658 of Hansard, when he said this:

PUBLIC WORKS-PORT McNEILL, B.C.- REQUEST FOR BREAKWATER CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to see that the Minister of Public Works is not here tonight because as Minister of Transport he visited the general area about which I want to raise this question. However, I am sure that the parliamentary secretary to the minister, to whom I have recently supplied a map of this area, will learn something from it and add his influence to what I hope will result from the question I am going to raise.
On April 5 I asked the Minister of Public Works whether he would endeavour to prevail upon his colleagues in the cabinet to provide a supplementary estimate for the construction of a breakwater at Port McNeill on Vancouver Island, I should say that this is the first occasion I have raised a question under this order involving proposed construction under the public works department, and I hope that the fact that I am doing so will serve to lend weight to the importance I attach to this matter.
I may say that it was with a great deal of regret that I had to advise the people of this area that this item was not in the estimates which were tabled for the current fiscal year. I was therefore not too surprised to find the lead headline in the next issue of the North Island Gazette, which is published in the neighbouring community of Alert Bay, read "Port McNeill Erupts!" The article went on to say:
Village council was thrown into turmoil at its meeting last week when it learned that the community's long-expected breakwater was not included in this year's estimates of the federal public works department.
I may say that their anticipation that such would be the case was based, in part at least, on a letter addressed to me by the Minister of Public Works, a copy of which I furnished the council, under date of June 9, 1966, in which the minister said, in part:
-it is proposed to consider an item in the 1967-68 estimates for the construction of a boat harbour at Port McNeill-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
While I tried to make it clear to them that that statement meant nothing more nor less than what it said, that there was in existence, of course, the Treasury Board process of examination of proposed estimates, nevertheless I had indicated that I felt reasonably optimistic that this item would be included in the construction program for this year and that it would in fact go forward. I also indicated that until the estimates were actually tabled this was the most definite statement that we could expect on this subject. Their disappointment is, in my view, not at all over-rated.
I should explain, Mr. Speaker, that this community on northern Vancouver Island has recently become an incorporated municipality, as have some other places on the north island. I recognize that here in Ottawa it is perhaps a little difficult to keep up with the very rapid expansion which has taken place on the northern part of Vancouver Island. I should point out that the federal government took over in 1964 a wharf which had been constructed by the owners of a logging camp, and it is really from this date that the rapid development of Port McNeill as a community with shopping centres, banks, a modern hotel, and so on and so forth, has taken place. It has now become the centre for the new regional high school for the school district of north Vancouver Island.
I am sure the minister is aware that the Prime Minister and all of the members from the province of British Columbia as well as the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of my own party have received representations from that area since the item failed to appear in the estimates. Wires were sent from the village of Port McNeill, from the Port McNeill and district chamber of commerce, from the school district, district No. 85, which represents a large consolidated school district covering the entire northern section of Vancouver Island, and also from the Port McNeill Women's Hospital Auxiliary. I should point out that the only hospital in the district at Alert Bay is dependent on water transportation from Port McNeill.
I also point out that there has now been established a regional level of government for north Vancouver Island known as the regional district of Mount Waddington. This body represents the entire northern area of Vancouver Island's incorporated and unincorporated communities. Its members say unanimously that the immediate construction of this breakwater is essential to the continuance of development of ordinary life in these parts of Vancouver Island. The local member

14816	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of the legislative assembly who also happens to be the minister concerned with municipal affairs in British Columbia, has agreed that this is true.
One of the best letters to be sent to the Prime Minister and to be made available to me is from a local minister of the United Church of Canada who says:
It is important for you to understand that this is not simply a pressure campaign based on the theory that "the squeaking wheel gets the grease." On the contrary, the need for a breakwater for Port McNeill is urgent and the many letters you have received from this community should be interpreted in this light.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a small matter. Ten or 12,000 people on the north end of Vancouver Island are concerned vitally with this facility as is evident from the many representations.
In 1871, when British Columbia entered confederation, its population was 36,247, all but 9,000 of whom were Indians. If 36,000 people were considered important enough to warrant the building of a railway to the Pacific coast, surely the 10,000 or 12,000 people on northern Vancouver Island warrant some consideration at this time.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-REMOVAL OF SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
AGRICULTURE-REMOVAL OF SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext:
My reason for taking part in this debate tonight is to ask the minister or his parliamentary secretary why the support was removed from the surplus milk shipped by fluid milk shippers of this country.
First, I would suggest we consider who is affected. It is the producer of fluid milk, who has put more effort and more investment into his dairy operation than any other dairy farmer. I do not want to detract from the efforts made by other milk producers, but it is the dairy producer who has had to produce the highest quality and maintain a supply throughout the 12 months of the year. This means extra expense, extra investment and additional equipment.
No milk producer can produce an equal quantity throughout the year without having surplus milk at some periods. It would be impossible. So a producer finds himself with different quantities on hand. Some might be shipping 50 per cent to a fluid milk market; others, 75 per cent. In any case a considerable quantity goes to a manufacturing plant as what is called surplus milk. It is with respect to this portion of his production that the support he received last year has been withdrawn. I maintain that the fluid milk producer is being discriminated against, and this had led to further difficulties for the reason I have mentioned.
It is true the producer may get a premium price for the milk sold on the fluid milk market. But if 50 per cent of his production goes to a surplus market without benefit of a support price he finds himself in the unenviable position of having to produce milk during a 12 months period without adequate compensation, in the final analysis getting no more than the other person. So the fluid milk producer is questioning whether he ought to continue to ship his milk to a fluid milk market.

April 11, 1967	COMMONS
I read in this morning's paper that the price of milk in Ontario is increasing, and I am sure this increase will be followed in Quebec and in the other provinces of Canada. Why should this be so? It is because the fluid milk shipper is not getting support for his surplus. Other prices are advancing, so he is asking a higher price. It is suggested that the price of milk will advance by two cents a quart. I maintain this situation is brought about because of the insecurity of the fluid milk shipper. So this question affects the price of milk across the country, and as one involved in the dairy enterprise, I hate to see what is happening. I do not like to see the price of milk keep on advancing. I do not wish to see the price of anything keep on advancing. The cost of living is going up, and this is one more step.
I say there is no surplus. We have been importing butter, and that does not put us in a surplus position. I maintain that the minister and the government must take some action or further trouble will develop. My remarks are not intended to be critical. I hope what I am saying is constructive criticism. I also hope something will be done before it is too late, because already there have been threats to dump milk if the farmers do not get the proper price. I hope none of us see any milk dumped in Canada because I think that would be a sin. It would be something to be ashamed of in a starving world.
I do not like to say that the minister does not understand, but I am beginning to realize that he is not a farmer. He is a minister of agriculture learning as best he can. I would not like to say he does not care, because I think he does. I only hope he takes some action before it is too late. This thing has gone beyond the point of pushing it around in the House of Commons. It is time some action was taken.
Farmers across the country are getting older and older. I was talking to a cheese factory operator yesterday and he told me his production of cheese is down 25,000 pounds in the first quarter of this year, and he has no reason to think that this decrease will not continue throughout the year. As I say, our farmers are getting older, and they are getting tired of a seven day week operation.
As a result of my few remarks I hope the minister will give some consideration to this problem I have many documents on my desk which I can show him to establish that some farmers are shipping two thirds of their milk to a manufacturing plant, and the present situation is pretty difficult for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-REMOVAL OF SUPPORT PRICE FOR MANUFACTURING MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Hastings-South (Mr. Grills) for bringing this important matter to the attention of the minister and the house. I can assure him, as one who has produced fluid milk for an important market, that the government is quite conscious of the fact that there are additional costs attached to the production of fluid milk and that there is a difficulty in maintaining continuity of supply.
There is, however, an important feature, in that we must determine the jurisdiction under which each of these areas falls. In the first place, fluid milk is produced according to provincial requirements and regulations. It is hauled in vehicles that come under provincial jurisdiction, and provincial governments are generally regarded to have accepted, and they themselves have accepted, the responsibility for fluid milk.
On the other hand we feel that manufacturing milk, part of which goes into an export trade, is our responsibility, and it has been agreed that it is the responsibility of the federal government. I think probably the federal government has assumed its full responsibility in measuring up to a very satisfactory degree, but maybe not to the full aspirations of the producers of manufacturing milk.
I only want to mention three salient points in connection with the federal policy. The first of course is that these jurisdictions have been defined. Second, $120 million has been appropriated to the Canadian Dairy Commission to assist in the establishment of a satisfactory price for manufacturing milk f.o.b. factory, and I would like to say that this is based on a buying price for butter of 63 cents per pound, and 20 cents for powder. This means approximately $4.75 f.o.b. factory to the farmers, and this is considerably more than has prevailed in recent years and recent months.
While the policy is not all that might be desired, I regret on behalf of the minister that we are unable to meet the requirements of the hon. member for Hastings South in suggesting we should further support fluid milk prices. This is clearly the responsibility of the provincial governments.
