maintopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March 22, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) announced the dairy policy of the Canadian government to the effect that deficiency payments to milk producers would be raised to $1.21 per hundredweight, which would bring the price of milk to $4.75 f.o.b. factory. And the minister went on to say that there would be a 10-cent deduction per hundredweight for export costs.
As pointed out by one government member, it was really an increase but I suggest that increase was far below what was asked the day before by the thousand delegates who came to Ottawa from all parts of the province of Quebec to make their grievances known to their members of parliament and to appeal to the cabinet.
At the time, various regional associations of dairy producers were heard through their president, but the man who explained the farm problems more fully was without question Mr. Lionel Saurel, president of C.F.U., who summarized the tragic situation in which the farmers find themselves.
He did an excellent job; the farmers were proud of their president and all hon. members present listened attentively.
Mr. Saurel did not use high-sounding words; he gave the facts.
Even the Minister of Agriculture was impressed by his sincerity, because while Mr. Saurel was talking he managed to say to the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve) who was sitting next to him; If he could be with us to convince the others.
Those words were repeated to the 1,000 farmers by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development when he was asked to speak to them.
At some other point during the meeting, the minister spoke to them again, this time without being invited to do so. He told them not to worry any more, that although he himself, a city dweller, did not know much about the situation, the government had many experts who already were aware of it.
It was after meeting one of those experts that I decided certains facts should be pointed out. The said expert seemed confined to 1963, at which time the Conservatives made way for the Liberals.
This person told me that milk was then sold at $2.66, while today the price is $4.65.

Mr. Speaker, if experts can amuse themselves by making comparisons, I shall do the same. I should like to remind the parliamentary secretary to the hon. minister that in 1950, milk was sold at only $2 per hundredweight, but at that time, I repeat, a tractor cost $1,200 or $1,500. Now, to buy a tractor we have to pay $4,500 to $5,000. But let it go, as far as the tractor is concerned, since one only buys every ten years. However, in the case of meal and fertilizers which farmers buy seven months a year to feed their cattle, the price difference is still the same.
For example, today, for barley, oats and corn, the farmer pays $3.75, whereas he only paid $1.25 per hundredweight in 1950.
The farmer now pays $4 or $4.25 per hundredweight for bran and shorts which are just by-products of wheat, while in 1950 he paid only $1.25 or $1.35.
Knowing that the hon. minister is about to revise his policy, I hope that the 300 per cent increases on machinery and meal will be taken into account.
When the minister strongly hopes that Mr. Saurel will be at his side to convince the others whom does he have in mind? Who are those cabinet members opposed to the new dairy policy?
Personally, I thought that inadequate funds explained the inadequacy of the dairy policy. I am reassured in reading the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 43 of the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs sitting on Monday, February 6, 1967, on page 3000.
This involves the Minister of Finance and Receiver General who was replying to a question by a member and I take the liberty of quoting the question and answer. The member asked:
Mr. Sharp-Do you feel that at present in Canada the money supply is sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Shall I put it this way? I believe that during the term that I have been in office the money supply has been sometimes more than adequate for the purpose.
The member asked:
I would just like to ask the minister to repeat his last answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
I have not been concerned about a deficiency of money and credit. I may be concerned about that in the future but during my year or so in office I have not been concerned about that problem.
In view of the fact that finance could not influence the Minister of Agriculture in his dairy policy could the minister or the parliamentary secretary to the minister (Mr. Beer)
April 11, 1967	COMMONS
give, for the guidance of all farmers, the names of the cabinet members who hindered him in his work?
Since the minister has already expressed the wish of having at his side the president of the Catholic Farmers Union, in order to work up intrigues, could we know who are the others he was thinking about in a moment of sincerity?
It is essential that presidents and representatives of farmers unions or organizations apply to the right person if their intrigues are to be effective, and I hope that the freedom of action then given back to the Minister of Agriculture will enable him to review his dairy policy, while taking into account the price of tractors, and of feed grain. Since the indemnities of ministers and of house members have tripled, in all fairness, the price of milk should be increased to $6 per hundredweight, but the farmers are not asking that much. They are asking for $5. By accepting $5 per hundredweight, they are making a $1 gift to society, to consumers, whereas if the government adds $1 to the $4 granted last year, it is merely a payment on account of what it owes the farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion I regret first of all that I am unable to reply in the other official language, but I wish to thank the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) for his important question. Let me assure him that no one could be more sympathetic to the cost-price squeeze in which the farmer finds himself than the minister or I, personally. Probably all of these factors were taken into consideration by the minister when he insisted on an additional amount of money to support the dairy program. We must recognize that the amount of money allocated to the dairy support program has been increased by 33 J per cent for 1967-68 over that for 1966-67. I am sure the hon. member would be the first person to agree that this is a substantial step forward.
I regret of course that the $1.21 of federal money in respect of every 100 pounds of manufacturing milk is not sufficient to meet the need. It was the feeling of the minister that this increase represented a responsible step forward at this particular time, and all that the government and the minister saw fit to work into the program for this particular year. I am not aware that there will be any immediate review, but certainly as time progresses the policy will be reconsidered.
